title: Why Doctors Drilled Holes in Skulls
style: Stylized realistic 3D CGI animation still, high-end animated explainer look, Pixar-meets-realism, cinematic soft lighting, detailed skin, hair and fabric, expressive faces, shallow depth of field, no text, no letters, no gore, vertical 9:16 framing.

sections.name: Why Doctors Drilled Holes in Skulls

lines.prompt: A medieval barber-surgeon in a red tunic with a white ruff leans over a frightened man lying on his side on a wooden bed, a hand-crank drill touching the top of his head, bright blue sky behind

lines: For thousands of years, doctors had a cure for headaches. They drilled a hole in your head.

lines.prompt: Close-up of an ancient human skull on a stone table lit by torchlight, with a neat round hole in the top of it, an archaeologist's gloved hand pointing at it

lines: It's called trepanation, and it's the oldest surgery we know of. Skulls with holes go back thousands of years.

lines.prompt: A stone age healer in furs scraping at a patient's scalp with a flint tool beside a campfire, villagers watching from the shadows

lines: People did it to let out evil spirits, or to treat head injuries, fits and terrible headaches.

lines.prompt: Close-up of two ancient skulls side by side, one hole with smooth rounded healed edges, glowing soft highlight on the healed rim

lines: And here's the wild part. Many of these skulls show the bone grew back around the hole.

lines.prompt: A cheerful ancient villager with a small bandage wrapped around his head walking out of a hut into morning sunlight, waving

lines: That means a lot of patients actually survived, and lived for years afterwards.

lines.prompt: Modern neurosurgeon in blue scrubs in a clean operating room holding a small modern surgical drill, looking at a brain scan on a screen

lines: Surgeons still make holes in the skull today. They just call it a craniotomy, and they use anaesthetic.
